questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the enzyme that unwinds DNA during replication
questions.stem: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix during replication?

options.misconception: confuses the unwinding enzyme with the synthesizing enzyme
confuses unwinding with joining Okazaki fragments

questions.explanation: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs to unwind the double helix. DNA polymerase synthesizes new strands, ligase joins fragments, and primase makes RNA primers, so each distractor names a real replication enzyme applied to the wrong task.
questions.hint: Which enzyme separates the two strands?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: What does 'semiconservative replication' mean?

options.text: Each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new strand
Both strands in each new molecule are newly synthesized
Old and new DNA segments are mixed within each strand
The original DNA molecule remains unchanged and a copy is made
options.misconception: describes conservative replication rather than semiconservative

questions.explanation: In semiconservative replication, each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. The other options describe conservative or dispersive models, which do not match the established mechanism.
questions.hint: How many original strands remain in each daughter molecule?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Okazaki fragments are produced on which strand during DNA replication?

options.misconception: reverses leading and lagging strand synthesis

options.text: Both strands, because synthesis is always discontinuous
options.misconception: incorrectly generalizes discontinuous synthesis to both strands

options.text: Neither strand; fragments are RNA primers
options.misconception: confuses Okazaki fragments with RNA primers

questions.explanation: The lagging strand is synthesized in short Okazaki fragments because DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction while the template runs the other way. The leading strand is synthesized continuously.
questions.hint: Which strand cannot be synthesized continuously?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: state the direction of DNA synthesis
questions.stem: DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA in which direction?

options.misconception: reverses the direction of DNA synthesis

options.text: Either direction depending on the template
Both directions simultaneously on one strand
options.misconception: confuses polymerase activity with helicase unwinding

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' hydroxyl end of the growing strand, so synthesis always proceeds 5' to 3'. It cannot synthesize in the 3' to 5' direction.
questions.hint: To which end are new nucleotides added?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments
questions.stem: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments during DNA replication?

options.misconception: confuses fragment joining with strand elongation

questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand. The other enzymes perform unwinding, elongation, or primer synthesis instead.
questions.hint: Which enzyme seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Primase is required during DNA replication because:

options.text: It synthesizes RNA primers for DNA polymerase
It unwinds the double helix ahead of synthesis
It proofreads newly synthesized DNA strands
It seals nicks between Okazaki fragments

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase cannot start synthesis from scratch; primase makes short RNA primers that provide a 3' end for DNA polymerase to extend.
questions.hint: What does DNA polymerase need before it can begin?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Telomerase prevents chromosome shortening by:

options.text: Adding repetitive DNA sequences to chromosome ends
Joining sister chromatids at the centromere
options.misconception: confuses telomere maintenance with chromatid cohesion

options.text: Repairing double-strand breaks throughout the genome
options.misconception: confuses telomerase with DNA repair enzymes

options.text: Unwinding DNA at origins of replication

questions.explanation: Telomerase extends telomeres by adding repetitive sequences to chromosome ends, compensating for the end-replication problem. It does not repair breaks or unwind DNA.
questions.hint: What structure is at the very end of a chromosome?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: DNA replication in eukaryotes begins at:

options.text: Multiple origins of replication along each chromosome
A single origin at the centromere of each chromosome
The telomeres at both ends of each chromosome
options.misconception: confuses replication start sites with chromosome ends

options.text: Random positions determined by RNA primers
options.misconception: confuses origin selection with primer placement

questions.explanation: Eukaryotic chromosomes are large, so replication initiates at many origins along each chromosome to complete copying in a reasonable time. Primers are placed after origin recognition, not randomly.
questions.hint: Why would one origin per chromosome be too slow?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the enzyme that synthesizes RNA
questions.stem: Which enzyme synthesizes RNA from a DNA template?

options.misconception: confuses RNA synthesis with DNA synthesis
confuses RNA synthesis with protein synthesis

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and synthesizes a complementary RNA strand. DNA polymerase makes DNA, helicase unwinds, and ribosomes translate RNA into protein.
questions.hint: Which enzyme produces RNA rather than DNA or protein?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A promoter is a DNA sequence that:

options.text: Provides a binding site for RNA polymerase
Codes for a specific amino acid
options.misconception: confuses regulatory sequence with coding sequence

questions.explanation: A promoter is a regulatory DNA region where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription. Terminators end transcription, coding sequences specify amino acids, and splicing removes introns.
questions.hint: Where does transcription begin?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A codon consists of:
questions.explanation: A codon is a three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA that specifies one amino acid or a stop signal. It is not a single nucleotide, base pair, or whole mRNA molecule.
questions.hint: How many nucleotides specify one amino acid?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: The anticodon on a tRNA molecule pairs with:

options.misconception: confuses anticodon with amino acid attachment site

questions.explanation: The tRNA anticodon is complementary to an mRNA codon, allowing the tRNA to deliver the correct amino acid during translation. It does not pair with DNA, an amino acid, or rRNA.
questions.hint: What nucleic acid carries codons to the ribosome?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: During translation, the A site of a ribosome is where:

options.misconception: describes the P site instead of the A site
describes the E site instead of the A site

questions.explanation: The A site accepts incoming aminoacyl-tRNA. The P site holds the tRNA attached to the growing polypeptide, and the E site is where deacylated tRNA exits. mRNA is not degraded at the A site.
questions.hint: What enters the ribosome during elongation?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Which codon typically initiates translation?

options.misconception: selects a common codon rather than start codon

questions.explanation: AUG codes for methionine and serves as the start codon in most mRNAs. UAA is a stop codon, while UUU and GUA code for other amino acids and do not initiate translation.
questions.hint: Which codon also specifies methionine?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Stop codons function during translation by:

options.text: Signaling release of the completed polypeptide
Adding a final amino acid to the chain
options.misconception: confuses stop codons with sense codons
confuses translation termination with transcription initiation

questions.explanation: Stop codons are not recognized by tRNAs; release factors bind and trigger release of the completed polypeptide from the ribosome. They do not add amino acids or start transcription.
questions.hint: What happens when the ribosome reaches the end of the coding sequence?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A missense mutation changes a codon so that it:

options.text: Removes a nucleotide from the sequence

questions.explanation: A missense mutation is a point mutation that substitutes one amino acid for another in the protein. Silent, nonsense, and frameshift mutations produce different outcomes.
questions.hint: What changes in the protein sequence?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A silent mutation does not alter the amino acid sequence because:

options.text: DNA repair enzymes correct it before translation
options.misconception: attributes silence to repair rather than code redundancy

options.text: The mutation occurs in noncoding DNA
options.misconception: confuses silent mutation with mutation outside coding region

options.text: tRNA anticodons are flexible enough to ignore it
options.misconception: overstates wobble pairing as the sole explanation

questions.explanation: Multiple codons can specify the same amino acid, so some nucleotide changes do not change the protein. Redundancy of the genetic code is the primary reason a mutation can be silent.
questions.hint: Can different codons code for the same amino acid?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A nonsense mutation is most likely to produce:

options.text: A protein with one substituted amino acid
An extended protein with extra amino acids
options.misconception: confuses premature stop with loss of stop

questions.explanation: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon, causing translation to terminate early and usually yielding a shortened, nonfunctional protein.
questions.hint: What does a premature stop codon do?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A frameshift mutation results from:

options.text: Insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of three
Substitution of one nucleotide for another

options.misconception: confuses gene-level frameshift with chromosomal abnormality

questions.explanation: Frameshifts occur when insertions or deletions shift the reading frame because their length is not a multiple of three. Substitutions may change one codon, and chromosomal changes are larger-scale alterations.
questions.hint: How many nucleotides make up one codon?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: The central dogma of molecular biology describes information flow from:

options.misconception: reverses the direction of information flow
describes reverse transcription pathway as general rule
starts with protein, violating central dogma

questions.explanation: The central dogma states that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA during transcription and from RNA to protein during translation. Reverse flow is not the general rule.
questions.hint: What is the usual order of DNA, RNA, and protein?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: An organism's genotype refers to its:
questions.explanation: Genotype is the set of alleles an organism carries. Phenotype is the observable result, which can also be influenced by environment and is not limited to chromosome number.
questions.hint: Which term describes the alleles present?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that:

options.text: Allele pairs separate during gamete formation
Alleles for different traits assort independently
Dominant alleles always mask recessive alleles

questions.explanation: Segregation means the two alleles for a gene separate so each gamete receives one. Independent assortment, dominance, and blending are related but distinct concepts.
questions.hint: What happens to allele pairs when gametes form?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Independent assortment is most directly observed when:

options.text: Genes are closely linked on one chromosome
options.misconception: describes linkage, opposite of independent assortment

options.text: A single gene has multiple alleles

questions.explanation: Genes on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis. Linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together unless crossing over separates them.
questions.hint: Which chromosome arrangement allows free recombination?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Incomplete dominance produces a phenotype that is:

options.text: Intermediate between the two parental phenotypes
A simultaneous expression of both parental phenotypes
options.misconception: describes codominance rather than incomplete dominance

options.text: Absent because the trait is recessive

questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote shows a blended or intermediate phenotype. Codominance shows both phenotypes together, and complete dominance masks the recessive allele.
questions.hint: What does a red-and-white flower cross look like?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A sex-linked recessive trait is more commonly expressed in males because:

options.text: Males have only one X chromosome
The Y chromosome carries the trait

options.misconception: incorrectly states females do not carry X-linked genes

questions.explanation: Males are XY and have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on that X is expressed. Females have two X chromosomes and need two recessive alleles.
questions.hint: How many X chromosomes do males have?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Epigenetic changes can affect gene expression by:

options.text: Modifying DNA or histones without changing sequence
Replacing nucleotides in the DNA sequence
Translating mRNA into a different protein

questions.explanation: Epigenetics involves chemical modifications such as methylation or histone changes that alter expression without changing the DNA sequence. Mutations, chromosomal deletions, and translation are separate processes.
questions.hint: Does the DNA sequence itself change?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: The two strands of DNA are antiparallel because:

options.text: They run in opposite 5' to 3' directions
They have complementary base sequences only
options.misconception: identifies complementarity but not strand direction

options.text: They are connected by hydrogen bonds

options.misconception: incorrectly claims strands use different sugars

questions.explanation: Antiparallel means the strands run in opposite directions, one 5' to 3' and the other 3' to 5'. Complementarity and hydrogen bonding are separate features, and both strands use deoxyribose.
questions.hint: What does 'antiparallel' describe?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify RNA base pairing with adenine
questions.stem: In RNA, which base pairs with adenine?

options.misconception: pairs adenine with the wrong pyrimidine

questions.explanation: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine, so adenine pairs with uracil in RNA. Thymine pairs with adenine in DNA, while cytosine and guanine pair with each other.
questions.hint: Which base replaces thymine in RNA?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Peptide bonds form between:

options.text: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and amino group of another
The side chains (R groups) of adjacent amino acids
options.misconception: locates bond in side chains rather than backbone

options.text: The phosphate groups of tRNA molecules
options.misconception: confuses amino acid linkage with tRNA chemistry

options.text: The nitrogenous bases of mRNA codons
options.misconception: confuses protein synthesis with nucleic acid structure

questions.explanation: A peptide bond is an amide bond between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, forming the protein backbone. Side chains, tRNA phosphates, and mRNA bases are not linked this way.
questions.hint: Which functional groups react during protein synthesis?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A mutagen is best defined as:

options.text: An agent that increases mutation rate
An enzyme that repairs DNA damage
A gene that suppresses cell division

questions.explanation: A mutagen is any physical or chemical agent that raises the frequency of mutations. Repair enzymes, tumor suppressors, and transcription factors perform different biological roles.
questions.hint: What causes mutations to occur more often?
